chunks.text: Op-ed · 7 min read · By The Muntin Desk

Four loyalty models compete for the independent restaurant operator’s setup time and monthly fee. Three of them don’t pay back. One does, but only when the kitchen is already running a healthy direct channel. Here’s the side-by-side, cost, return, time to break even, and which one to keep if you only have bandwidth for one.
In short

Four loyalty models compete for an independent operator’s setup time: paper punch cards, integrated P O S loyalty (Toast/Square), standalone platforms (Fivestars/Como), and Crm-direct (Mailchimp/Klaviyo + own checkout). P O S-integrated loyalty has published monthly pricing (Toast Rewards is roughly 50 dollars/month; Square Loyalty starts at 25 dollars/month); standalone platforms do not publish open pricing.

Punch cards have the strongest percentage return on a small base; Crm-direct has the strongest absolute return when the direct channel already converts; standalone platforms tend to under-perform on percentage terms because the cost structure is high relative to the behavioral lift.
The loyalty conversation is downstream of the channel conversation, fix the channel first, layer the loyalty after, on the direct surface where margin can fund a real customer relationship.

I ran two of these programs for over a year on the same restaurant, then dropped both and replaced them with a third. The numbers below are mine, not industry benchmarks. Your conversion rates and average check will differ. The order of magnitude is what carries the argument: the gap between the best and worst model isn’t 20%, it’s 4x.
The four models in play.
Every loyalty program a US independent restaurant runs fits one of four shapes. The implementations differ; the underlying economics don’t. Walk through them in order of operator cost-to-implement.

Cost-to-implement is the wrong axis to rank these on, because the cheapest model and the most expensive one are both live answers depending on the channel you already run. The axis that actually decides it is annual kept margin, the dollars the program returns after its own cost. On a roughly 500-customer base, in my own operator practice, the spread is the whole argument: the best model returns close to nine times the worst one still worth running. These are illustrative figures from one restaurant, not industry benchmarks.

Annual kept margin by loyalty model on a roughly five-hundred-customer base, illustrative operator figures from one restaurant. Crm plus direct returns the most: a mid-point near six thousand five hundred dollars a year on a band of five to eight thousand. P O S-integrated loyalty returns about two thousand four hundred dollars a year. Paper punch cards return about seven hundred fifty dollars a year on essentially no cost. Standalone platforms publish no open pricing and, in operator practice, return the worst margin per dollar of the four, shown in rust as the worst case rather than a measured bar. A benchmark tick marks the roughly one-thousand-dollar-a-year line below which a program is not worth the operator's setup time.
Why the Crm-direct path wins by 2x.

The three competitor models, punch cards, P O S loyalty, standalone loyalty platforms, share a structural problem. They all treat every customer the same. The frequent guest who already comes in every week gets the same 10%-off-after-10-visits offer as the once-a-quarter customer who needs an entirely different intervention. The reward is undifferentiated, so the spend is undifferentiated, so the margin lift is mediocre across the board.

The Crm-direct path lets you segment. A weekly regular gets early access to the chef’s upcoming tasting menu and zero discounts, they don’t need a discount, they need to feel known. A lapsed customer who hasn’t visited in 60 days gets a specific 15 dollars-off-your-next-visit email at day 58 (right before they’d normally lapse to 90+ days). A first-time direct buyer gets a thank-you with their next-time-save offer. Three customers, three different interventions, three different margin profiles. That’s where the 2x comes from.
Why the punch card still beats the standalone platform on R O I.

This is the one that surprises most operators. The punch card costs essentially nothing, ten dollars a year for printing, and produces a real, if small, behavioral lift in repeat visits. Even modest absolute returns make the percentage return enormous. The standalone loyalty platform produces somewhat larger absolute returns, but its cost structure is contact-for-quote (Fivestars and Como do not publish open pricing) and historically lands well above the P O S-integrated tier, high enough relative to the behavioral lift that the percentage return is materially worse than either the punch card or P O S loyalty. If 200 dollars/month is on the table for customer marketing, it’s rarely best-spent on the standalone platform; the same 200 dollars goes further almost anywhere else.

The integrated P O S loyalty sits between the two: the cost is low enough that the modest behavioral lift still pays back, but only just, and the data is owned by the P O S vendor, so it doesn’t come with you when you switch processors.

A decision tree for picking a loyalty model. First question: do you have a direct online channel that already converts? If yes, run Crm plus direct, Klaviyo or Mailchimp wired to your own Stripe, Toast, or Square checkout, with a segmented automation that fires at day fifty-eight. Five thousand to eight thousand dollars in kept margin on a five-hundred-customer base, monthly cost fifty to one-twenty. If no direct channel: second question, are you already running P O S loyalty like Toast Rewards or Square Loyalty? If yes, keep it, do not pay a standalone platform on top. Break-even at four months, twenty-four hundred in kept margin per year, the data is stranded when you switch processors but it is real data. If no P O S loyalty either: third question, do you have a barista or a counter where every transaction is in-person? If yes, run paper punch cards. Ten dollars per year, seven hundred fifty in kept margin, break-even in three weeks, and the kitchen learns to track repeat behavior. If no in-person counter and no direct channel: stop. The loyalty conversation is downstream of the channel conversation. Fix the channel first.
What this means for your setup.

If you have a direct channel that’s already converting: run the Crm-direct path. Klaviyo for the segmentation; your own Stripe/Toast/Square checkout for the order data; a manually-curated regulars list for the highest-value 50 customers; automated re-engagement at day 58. Vendor-published monthly cost runs 20 dollars, 120 dollars depending on email send volume and platform tier. Margin lift in year one varies widely by restaurant; operators with healthy direct channels report the strongest returns of any of the four models in this comparison.

If you don’t have a direct channel: run paper punch cards while you build one. The 750 dollars/year is real money, and the punch card teaches your kitchen staff to track repeat behavior in a way that pays off when you eventually migrate to the Crm-direct path. Don’t spend the 200 dollars/month on a standalone loyalty platform thinking it’s the bridge, it isn’t. It’s a worse-margin version of the punch card with extra complexity.

If you’re already running P O S loyalty: keep it. The break-even is reasonable and the data is real, even if the data is owned by your P O S vendor and gets stranded when you switch processors. Just don’t pay the standalone platform on top of it, that’s a double-spend with overlapping returns.

That ordering matters more than the model choice, because each step funds the one after it. Layering a paid loyalty platform onto a broken channel just meters spend against a leak. Here is the sequence I run, and the gate that has to clear before the next step earns its monthly fee.

The order to build loyalty in, because each stage funds the next. Step one, fix the channel: get a direct online ordering or reservation flow that converts, so guest data lands in something you own rather than a third-party app. This is the gate; until it clears, every paid loyalty layer just meters spend against a leak. Step two, capture the customer: a punch card at the counter or an email line at checkout costs near nothing and teaches the kitchen to track repeat behavior while the channel matures. Step three, segment on the data you now own: split weekly regulars from lapsed sixty-day guests and treat them differently, which is where the Crm plus direct path earns its two-times return. Step four, automate the re-engagement: a day-fifty-eight lapsed-guest email and a curated top-fifty regulars list, the highest-margin move, but only once the three steps under it are real.
Don Goldstein is a restaurant operator and runs Muntin Digital . The four-model comparison above is from running each variant on the same restaurant between twenty twenty-four and twenty twenty-five.

Key takeaways

Standalone loyalty platforms (Fivestars, Como) do not publish open pricing, both are contact-for-quote. Historically they land well above the P O S-integrated tier, which makes the percentage return weak against either the punch card or P O S loyalty.
P O S-integrated loyalty (Toast Rewards, Square Loyalty) sits in the middle on cost but the data is owned by your processor, it doesn’t come with you if you switch.

The Crm-direct path wins because it lets you segment: weekly regulars get tasting-menu invites with no discount, lapsed customers get a 15 dollars-off email at day 58, first-time direct buyers get a thank-you with a next-visit offer.
Don’t pay both a standalone platform and a P O S-integrated loyalty, that’s a double-spend with overlapping returns.
If your channel mix is wrong (mostly third-party app orders, no direct flow), no loyalty layer fixes it; fix the channel first.
